Let’s talk about something that still shapes leadership today—especially when it comes to women: gender, scrutiny, and the glass ceiling.
When you step into a leadership role, you expect challenges. But for women, those challenges come with a higher price tag. Think back to the 2016 campaign—every gesture, every word, was under a microscope. The expectations? They were often impossible. Be strong, but don’t be too strong. Be warm, but not too emotional. It’s not just a figure of speech—the glass ceiling is real, built up by both subtle bias and, sometimes, open hostility.
Imagine being the first woman to win a major party’s nomination. There’s this rush of pride, breaking new ground. But there’s also this sense of standing alone, every move watched and judged. The scrutiny never let up, and sometimes, it felt like no amount of effort could ever be enough.
On the campaign trail, these double standards popped up everywhere. Picture a small town meeting—supporters gathering, talking honestly about what working families are up against. People share their struggles, their dreams. But even in those moments, you could feel a thread of doubt in the air. Some wondered if a woman could really understand their problems. Or they questioned if she was “likable” enough to lead. Have you ever felt like you needed to prove yourself in ways others didn’t?
Then there’s the media. Instead of focusing on policies or experience, coverage often zeroed in on appearance, tone, or whether someone smiled enough. Social media only made it louder, spreading rumors and criticism faster than ever. And this didn’t just affect the candidate—it wore down supporters and staff, too.
Sexism wasn’t always obvious. Sometimes it was a so-called joke, or a side comment about “likability.” Other times, it was more subtle—a sense that certain rooms were closed off, that some opportunities just weren’t on the table. The pressure to be perfect never stopped, and every mistake seemed bigger than it should have been.
But here’s what really mattered: moments of connection and support. Women from all backgrounds reached out, sharing their own stories of fighting and overcoming. Those small acts of solidarity—they meant everything. They reminded us that the push for equality wasn’t just about one person, or even one campaign. It was about all of us, together.
The glass ceiling didn’t shatter in 2016. But you know what? It cracked. That experience showed both the progress we’ve made, and how much farther we still have to go. This journey wasn’t just about one leader—it was about opening doors for everyone who comes next.
